Notes: 毛 (máo) means fine hair or fur, here the trivial detail; 毛病 is a small fault that keeps recurring. It stretches across a machine that breaks down, a person's annoying habit, and a minor recurring ailment, all the everyday senses of "something is wrong with it."

Notes: On Contradiction: Mao Zedong's 1937 philosophical essay applying materialist dialectics to political analysis. One of the two foundational texts of Mao Zedong Thought (alongside 实践论 Shíjiàn Lùn, "On Practice").

Moutai: the prestige baijiu produced in Maotai Town, Guizhou province. Made from sorghum using the sauce-aroma (酱香 jiàngxiāng) method, it is the most famous Chinese spirit and functions as a currency of respect in formal Chinese business culture.

Notes: 茅 máo (thatch grass) + 屋 wū (dwelling). A simple hut roofed with grass. The 茅屋 is a literary image of humble, virtuous poverty , the dwelling of the reclusive scholar or hermit.

English: to pop up; to suddenly emerge

Notes: 没(有) is the standard negator for completed actions. It replaces 了 entirely , you never say 没吃了, because 没 already carries the information that no completion occurred. The 了 is superfluous and wrong. This is a near-universal rule: 没 and post-verb 了 are mutually exclusive.
没 méi (not have) + 错 cuò (error). "No error here," used to agree firmly: 没错，我就是这个意思 "exactly, that's just what I mean." Often softened to 没错儿 in northern speech.
Tags: meaning daily-life communication characters daily spoken language etiquette focus cleft past

Notes: 没 méi (lack; without) + 道理 dàolǐ (reason; logic). "Without reason": lacking the logic or justice to be acceptable. Used when something is not just inconvenient but genuinely wrong in its reasoning or fairness.

English: it doesn't matter; never mind; that's okay
Notes: One of the most indispensable phrases in Mandarin. The standard response to 对不起 (sorry). Literally "no relationship" , meaning "it has no effect on us; it carries no weight." Learn this before your first week of speaking Chinese.
Tags: negation past-tense grammar particles social connections culture

Notes: 没 méi (lacks; does not have) + 礼貌. The standard rebuke. Heavier than English "rude" because it implies a failure of formation, not just a momentary lapse.

English: to lose face; to be embarrassed; without prestige
Notes: To be without face , whether because one has lost it through embarrassing behavior or because one's status is insufficient to command it. 没面子 is the social embarrassment register, distinct from the moral shame of 丢脸.

English: nothing / it's nothing / no big deal
Notes: 没 + 什么 (what; anything). 没什么 = "nothing; it's nothing." As a response to thanks or apologies: 没什么！= "No worries! / It's nothing!" Also as a statement: 冰箱里没什么吃的 "There's nothing much to eat in the fridge."

English: it's nothing; no problem; never mind; to be free (not busy)
Notes: 没 méi (not have) + 事 shì. "No matter." The everyday reassurance: it's fine, don't worry, no harm done. Also literally "to have nothing on," to be free.
One of the most useful everyday phrases, used to agree to a request, reassure, or confirm that something will be fine. Equivalent to "no problem / sure / consider it done." A warm, willing reply.

The negation of 有意思 , lacking appeal, engagement, or point. Can describe activities, conversations, people, or situations. Often used for mild complaint rather than outright criticism. 说没意思的话 (to say pointless things) is a common mild rebuke.

English: the ancestral temple — source of all Mazu worship
Notes: The Meizhou Ancestral Temple (湄洲祖庙) on Meizhou Island, Putian, Fujian, is the origin point of all Mazu temples worldwide. The first small temple was reportedly built at her grave site not long after her death in 987 CE. It has been expanded, burned, rebuilt, and expanded again across ten centuries.

English: every, each one of an identical series
Notes: 每 walks through a set member by member: 每个人 (every person), 每本书 (every book). It requires a measure word before the noun, with a short list of exceptions that are themselves measure-like: 每天, 每年, 每次 (day, year, time).
Tags: quantifiers adverb numbers measure-words classifiers nouns

Notes: 每天 měitiān: 每 měi (every; each) + 天 tiān (day). The neutral distributive "every day." 每 attaches to any time unit: 每年 (every year), 每月 (every month), 每周 (every week).

美 měi (beautiful; admirable) + 德. A beautiful virtue , a particular admirable quality, usable as a count noun. 谦虚是一种美德 "humility is a virtue." 中华民族的传统美德 "the traditional virtues of the Chinese nation" is one of the standard formulas in civic discourse.

美 měi + 感 gǎn (feeling; sense). The capacity to perceive and appreciate beauty. Used in art criticism, design, and discussions of taste. 有美感 "has a good aesthetic sense" · 缺乏美感 "lacks aesthetic awareness."
美 měi (beautiful) + 国 guó. From the phonetic transcription of "America" (亚美利加 Yà-Měi-lì-jiā), with 美 selected as both sound-match and flattering character. A lucky phonetic fit.

English: to beautify; to prettify; to whitewash
Notes: 美 měi (beautiful) + 化 huà (the -ize suffix). Literally "to make beautiful." 美化 covers both the literal beautifying of a place (planting flowers, cleaning streets) and the figurative dressing-up of something unattractive, that is, putting a flattering gloss on a person, a record, or a history.

美 měi + 丽 lì (splendid; brilliant , originally: a deer with fine antlers). Used for landscapes, natural scenes, and elevated emotional beauty. More literary than 漂亮. 美丽的风景 "beautiful scenery" · 美丽的心灵 "a beautiful soul."

English: miss (lit. beauty); address for a young woman

Notes: 美 měi (beautiful; excellent) + 食 shí (food; to eat). Fine food; delicacies. Used everywhere food culture is celebrated , travel blogs, TV shows, restaurant descriptions. 美食家 měishíjiā = gourmet; food connoisseur.

English: to go against one's conscience; to act in bad faith
Notes: 昧 mèi (to obscure; to violate knowingly). 昧良心 is the standard phrase for suppressing what one's conscience perceives and doing wrong anyway , the act Wang Yangming calls covering the sun with clouds.

English: spirit tablet — the ancestor's dwelling in the home
Notes: The spirit tablet (牌位, also 神主牌 shénzhǔpái or 祖先牌位 zǔxiān páiwèi) is a wooden or paper plaque inscribed with the ancestor's name, birth and death dates, and honorific. It is the material dwelling of the ancestor's spirit within the home or ancestral hall.

Notes: 盼 pàn (to long for, to expect) + 望 wàng (to look toward). To wait eagerly and warmly for something one cares about: 盼望已久 "long looked forward to." More emotional and yearning than 希望, it suggests an active, heartfelt waiting.

Notes: 旁 páng (side; beside) + 人 rén. Literally "people at the side": observers, onlookers, those not directly involved in a situation. The word carries a slightly theatrical quality: you, the protagonist, and 旁人 who watch. More literary than 别人. Common in classical and modern literary prose.

English: to jog; to run (as exercise); a run
Notes: 跑 + 步 (bù, step). The everyday verb-noun for running as exercise. Used both as an activity (我每天跑步, "I jog every day") and as a noun (一次跑步, "one running session"). The word covers everything from a casual neighborhood jog to marathon training.

跑 pǎo (run) + 出来 chūlái (come out). The full directional compound: running out of an enclosed space toward the speaker's position. The 来 anchors orientation , the speaker is outside, watching the emergence happen.

English: running track; runway (airport); a course of action
Notes: 跑 + 道 (dào, road; way; track). The physical track for running, the airport runway for planes, and , figuratively , a chosen course of professional or personal direction. 选择新的跑道 ("to choose a new track") is a near-fixed metaphor in career writing.

English: got away; ran off; (of fish, opportunity) escaped
Notes: 跑 + 了 (le, perfective particle). A small but very common construction marking that something or someone has escaped or slipped away. The subject is often something one wanted to keep: a thief, a debtor, a fish, a customer, an opportunity.

English: to brew tea; to steep tea
Notes: 泡 pào (to soak; to steep; to foam) + 茶 chá (tea). The everyday verb for making tea. 你喝什么茶？我去泡 "What tea would you like? I'll go steep it." Also: 泡茶时间 steeping time · 第一泡 the first infusion.

English: to risk one's life; to do something with everything one has
Notes: 拼 pīn (to throw together; to stake) plus 命. To "stake one's life" on something, used both literally (combat, rescue) and figuratively for any effort given without holding back. 拼命工作 "to work like one's life depends on it" is the standard phrase for sustained, all-in effort.

English: Pinyin; the phonetic spelling of Mandarin
Notes: 拼 pīn (to piece together) + 音 yīn (sound). The Romanized spelling that pieces a Mandarin syllable from initial, final, and tone. The scaffolding every learner climbs before the characters take hold.

Notes: 贫 (poor) + 困 (hard-pressed). Poverty seen as a wall that pens people in: not merely low income, but the trapped condition want creates. Formal register, common in policy and reporting.

English: moral character; the virtue a person has
Notes: 品 pǐn (rank; quality; character) + 德 dé. The grade of one's virtue. Where 道德 is morality in general, 品德 is the moral quality of a particular person. 品德高尚 "of lofty character" is the standard praise; 品德败坏 "of degraded character" is the standard condemnation.

English: safe and sound; at peace; well
Notes: 平 píng (calm) + 安 ān (safe). Safe and well, free of harm or trouble: 一路平安 "have a safe trip," 平安回家 "to get home safely." A staple of blessings and farewells.

Notes: 平 píng (level; plain) + 常 cháng (ordinary). Both an adjective (unremarkable, common) and a time word (in ordinary times, usually): 平常的一天 "an ordinary day," 我平常六点起床 "I usually get up at six."

Notes: 平 píng (level) + 地 dì (ground). Flat, even land, as opposed to slopes or mountains: 一片平地 "a stretch of level ground." The opposite is hilly or broken terrain.
平 píng (level) + 等 děng (rank). Equal standing, no rank set above another: 人人平等 "everyone is equal," 男女平等 "equality of men and women." More about status than about fairness in dealings.

English: average; on average; to even out
Notes: 平 píng (even) + 均 jūn (equal). The arithmetic mean, the level reached when a total is shared out evenly: 平均分 "average score," 平均年龄 "average age," 平均分配 "to distribute evenly."
平 píng (flat) + 面 miàn (surface; face). A flat surface, and in geometry a plane. Also the modifier in 平面设计 píngmiàn shèjì "graphic design," the flat, two-dimensional kind.

English: commoner; an ordinary person (vs the elite)
Notes: 平 píng (level, ordinary, common) + 民. An ordinary person without rank, wealth, or official position: the commoner as opposed to nobles, officials, or celebrities. 平民百姓 píngmín bǎixìng is a fixed pairing meaning the common folk, the man and woman in the street.
平 píng (level) + 稳 wěn (steady; firm). Moving or sitting on an even keel, without jolts or swings: 平稳着陆 "a smooth landing," 物价平稳 "prices are stable."
评 (to judge, comment) + 价 (worth). To weigh something and assign it a worth: a teacher's assessment, a customer's review, a verdict on a person's conduct. Works as both verb and noun.

English: to review, to comment; a review, a commentary
Notes: 评 píng (to appraise, to judge) + 论. To pass critical judgement on something, or the resulting commentary. A film review, a book review, a comment posted under an article (评论区 pínglùnqū "the comments section") are all 评论.
破 (to break, smash) + 坏 (to ruin). Two near-synonyms doubled for force. Destroys physical things (buildings, environment) and abstract ones alike (trust, an atmosphere, a plan, the rules).

Notes: 保佑 bǎoyòu = to protect and bless. The standard phrase spoken when lighting incense or making an offering at a temple or home shrine. Used across all levels of religious engagement, from deeply devout practitioners to secular cultural observers marking a family occasion.

心肠 xīncháng = the heart-and-gut, the moral center of a person. 菩萨心肠 describes someone of exceptional compassion and forgiveness , a person who cannot bear to see others suffer and who gives without calculation.

English: the uncarved block — original simplicity before social shaping
Notes: 朴 pǔ: unworked wood, the block before the sculptor's chisel. The Daoist image for the original undivided state of human nature and reality, before categories, distinctions, desires, and social roles have carved it into something particular.

Pudong: the eastern bank of the Huangpu River and its hinterland, designated a special economic development zone in 1990. Its skyline of supertall towers built since the 1990s is the visual symbol of reform-era China.

English: universal deliverance — community feast for the unnamed dead
Notes: 普 pǔ (universal; general) + 度 dù (to cross over; to ferry across; to deliver). A feast laid out publicly , on street corners, in courtyards, at temple forecourts , specifically for the hungry ghosts who have no living descendants to offer for them.

Notes: 普 pǔ (widespread; universal) + 通 (general; running throughout). Widespread and holding everywhere: the quality of being ordinary, the common case rather than the special one. 普通人 (an ordinary person), 普通话 (the common spoken standard, Mandarin).

English: the seven emotions and six desires; the full range of human feeling
Notes: 七情 (the seven emotions: joy, anger, sorrow, fear, love, aversion, desire) + 六欲 (the six desires of the senses). Together they name the complete inner life of a human being.

English: the Qixi Festival; the Chinese Valentine's Day
Notes: 七 qī + 夕 xī (evening). The seventh evening of the seventh lunar month, the annual meeting of the Weaver Girl (织女) and the Cowherd (牛郎). Once a women's festival for praying for skill in needlework (乞巧, "begging for cleverness"), it is now celebrated as a day for lovers.

七 qī + 月 yuè (month). July in the solar calendar. The seventh lunar month is the Ghost Month (鬼月), when the gates of the underworld are believed to open and spirits roam among the living; its fifteenth day is the Ghost Festival (中元节).

Notes: 期 qī (a fixed period) + 间 jiān (interval). A defined stretch of time, often used after an event to mean "during": 假期期间 "during the holidays," 会议期间 "in the course of the meeting."

English: to expect; expectation; to set hopes on
Notes: 期 qī (a set time, to anticipate) + 望 wàng (to look toward). To expect something of someone or some outcome, with a definite hope and often a standard behind it: 不要辜负大家的期望 "do not let down everyone's expectations." Weightier and more formal than 希望.

English: Duke Huan of Qi and Guan Zhong — the classical model of ruler and reforming minister
Notes: 齐桓公 Qí Huán Gōng (r. 685–643 BCE) became the dominant power of the early Spring and Autumn through the administrative genius of his minister 管仲 Guǎn Zhòng. The partnership became the canonical Chinese example of a ruler who provides authority and a minister who provides competence.

English: complete (in range); all there; fully stocked
Notes: 齐 qí (even; all present) + 全 quán (complete). Said of a set or selection where every needed item is on hand: 设备齐全 "fully equipped," 品种齐全 "a complete range of varieties." Stresses that nothing in the expected range is missing.

其 qí (that; those) + 次 cì (order; rank; next). "Next in that sequence" , used to introduce the second point in a ranked list, following 首先 shǒuxiān (first of all) or 第一 dì yī. Slightly more formal than 然后 ránhòu, which is purely sequential.

其 qí (that; those) + 他 tā (other). "Those others" , anything outside the named set. The variant 其它 qítā uses the non-human 它 and is preferred when referring to things rather than people, though in practice 其他 covers both.

English: the rest; the remainder; the others
Notes: 其 qí (those) + 余 yú (remainder; surplus; what is left). "Those that remain" , refers to everything in a set that has not already been specified. More formal than 其他; 其余 often implies a complete remainder (everything else), while 其他 may just mean "various others."

其 qí (its; that) + 中 zhōng (middle; within). "Within that" or "among them" , used to pick out elements from a previously named set. One of the most frequent formal connectives in written Chinese, where English might say "of these" or "among which."

English: cheongsam — Manchu-derived dress, distinct from hànfú

Notes: 企 qǐ (to stand on tiptoe; to aspire) + 业 yè (undertaking). A business organization: 国有企业 "state-owned enterprise," 私营企业 "private enterprise," 企业家 "entrepreneur." The standard term for a firm as a legal and economic body.

English: to draft (a document); to draw up
Notes: 起 qǐ (to begin; to raise) + 草 cǎo (draft). To compose the first version of a formal text, a contract, law, speech, or plan. 起草合同 "to draft a contract."
Order-starting quantity, often per colour or per SKU rather than per order. Ask which. Factories will usually trade a lower MOQ for a higher unit price.
起 (to rise) plus 飞 (to fly): to rise into flight. Used literally of aircraft leaving the runway and figuratively of an economy or career that is about to surge.

起 (to rise; to stand up) + 义 (righteousness). The act of rising against an unjust authority, with 义 marking the moral legitimacy of the act. In Chinese historiography and political vocabulary, 起义 is the standard term for revolts understood as righteous from the inside.

English: the cause; what set something off
Notes: 起 qǐ (to rise; to start) + 因 yīn (cause). The cause that started a chain of events, the spark that set a matter in motion: 事情的起因 "the origin of the matter."

气 qì + 场 chǎng (field, as in electromagnetic field or a venue). Originally a TCM and qigong term for the field of qi that radiates from a practitioner. Absorbed into popular culture as a way of describing the palpable aura of a charismatic person. 气场强 = powerful aura; 气场弱 = weak presence.

气 qì + 愤 fèn (indignation; righteous anger, from the image of qi pressing against the heart). Slightly stronger and more formal than 生气. Implies that the anger is justified, that you are responding to something genuinely unfair or wrong. Less colloquial, more dignified.

气 qì + 候 hòu (season; to wait; signs). 候 originally referred to the five-day intervals used in classical Chinese to track seasonal changes. 气候 is the patterned behavior of atmospheric qi over time: climate, not weather. Also used metaphorically: 政治气候 (political climate).

Notes: With 结石 (jiéshí, stones, unmelted particles) and 冷纹 (lěngwén, cold marks), the visual defects to agree limits for, by size and number per piece.

气 qì + 色 sè (color; appearance). In TCM, the complexion (the color and quality of the face) is a direct index of the health of one's internal qi. 气色好 (good complexion) = qi is ample and circulating freely; 气色差 (poor complexion) = qi is deficient or blocked. A doctor's first diagnostic tool.

English: momentum; imposing presence; force of spirit
Notes: 气 qì + 势 shì (power; momentum; force, the potential energy of a situation). The directed force of qi, outward projection of power rather than inner refinement (气质). An army, a waterfall, a master calligrapher's brushstroke, a confident leader entering a room: all can have 气势.

气 qì (air; atmospheric qi) + 温 wēn (warmth; temperature). The temperature of the air, a meteorological and everyday term. Used in weather reports, health advice, and daily conversation about the feel of a day.

气 qì (breath; vital energy) + 韵 yùn (resonance; rhyme; musical tone). The first and supreme of Xie He's Six Principles: 气韵生动 qìyùn shēngdòng, "spirit resonance, life movement." A painting that has 气韵 is alive; one that lacks it is mere skilled craft.
Tags: arts nature taoism aesthetics classical calligraphy art brush writing history culture visual literary

English: spirit resonance and vitality — the supreme aesthetic criterion
Notes: Spirit resonance, life movement , Xie He first principle of painting, and the supreme criterion by which Chinese paintings are judged. A work with 气韵生动 has a quality of living presence that cannot be reduced to technical competence. It is the highest praise in Chinese art criticism.
Tags: art brush calligraphy culture history classical arts

Notes: 气 qì + 质 zhì (substance; essence; nature). The essential quality of a person's qi, their innate temperament and the bearing it produces. In psychological Chinese, it corresponds to personality type. In everyday speech, 有气质 means "has an air about them": elegant, distinctive, refined.

English: through all the ages; eternal; (of the dead) for ever
Notes: 千 qiān + 古 gǔ (antiquity; old). All the ages of history, time out of mind. 千古名句 is a line famous through the ages; 千古罪人 (a sinner for all time) is someone whose crime history will never forget.

English: a thousand li; a great distance
Notes: 千 qiān + 里 lǐ (the Chinese mile). Literally a thousand li, but in practice any great distance. 千里迢迢 qiānlǐ tiáotiáo describes a long, arduous journey from far away.

English: from a thousand li away; across a great distance
Notes: 千里 (a thousand li) + 迢迢 (tiáotiáo, remote, far off , a reduplication conveying long distance and weariness). The compound evokes a journey undertaken across great distance with effort and determination.

English: a connection across a thousand miles; long-distance destined bond
Notes: 千里 qiānlǐ = a thousand li (the traditional Chinese unit of distance; figuratively: any great distance). The phrase evokes connections that transcend physical separation , the meeting of people from far apart who nonetheless find each other.

English: a journey of a thousand li
Tags: chengyu classical idioms philosophy daoism daodejing laozi education learning

English: a thousand autumns; the ages; eternity
Notes: 千 qiān + 秋 qiū (autumn, here standing for a year). A thousand years, hence the long span of history and posterity. 千秋万代 (a thousand autumns, ten thousand generations) means for all time, down all future ages. 名垂千秋 is to have one's name endure through the ages.

English: ten million; by all means; absolutely (must / must not)
Notes: 千 qiān (thousand) + 万 wàn (ten-thousand), literally ten million. But its most common use is adverbial and emphatic, urging or warning with great force: 千万要小心 (you absolutely must be careful), 千万别忘了 (whatever you do, don't forget).
铅 qiān (lead) + 笔 bǐ. The everyday pencil, named for the old idea of a "lead" pencil even though the core is graphite. One of the first writing tools a child learns to name.

English: predecessor; senior; elder in one's field
Notes: 前 qián (before; preceding) + 辈 bèi (generation; people of the same era). Those of earlier generations who walked the path before you in your field, institution, or family. A term of respect: addressing someone as 前辈 acknowledges their experience and positions you as the newer arrival.

前 qián (former; preceding) + 朝 cháo (dynasty; court; morning). The dynasty that came before the current one , a term of historical reference used constantly in Chinese historical writing, since each dynasty defined itself partly in relation to what it replaced.

English: ahead; the forward direction; the front (military)
Notes: 前 qián (front) + 方 fāng (direction; area; square). A more formal and often grander term than 前面 , used in military contexts, official broadcasts, and literary or elevated speech. 前方记者 (correspondent at the front) is a journalism term.

English: to advance; to go forward; to march ahead

人 rén + 类 lèi (species; category; kind). Refers to humanity as a biological and civilizational category, the human species in its entirety across all time. Used in philosophical, scientific, and grand-historical registers. Much larger in scope than 人们, and without political coloring.

人 rén + 脉 mài (vein; pulse; artery, the channels through which blood flows). Your social and professional network, imagined as a circulatory system. 脉 is the same character used in 经脉 jīngmài (meridians) in TCM.

Notes: 人 rén + 们 men (plural suffix for animate nouns). A general, indefinite plural: "people" in the broad social sense, as in "one finds that people…" or "people say…" 们 cannot be combined with numbers; you cannot say ＊三人们. This plural is for social generality, not counting.

人 rén + 民 mín (common people; subjects; citizens). A politically weighted term. In the PRC context, it carries strong ideological resonance: the people as a collective subject and political actor, not merely a demographic count. Appears in major institutional names and slogans.

English: moral character; the quality of a person
Notes: 人 rén + 品 pǐn (quality; grade; character, three 口 mouths stacked, suggesting the spoken judgments of a community). The overall moral quality of a person as assessed by those around them: moral trustworthiness and reliability in relationships, not talent or intelligence.

English: human feeling; social obligation; the gift economy of favors
Notes: Human feeling, social obligation , the accumulated weight of favors, gifts, and consideration exchanged between people. To "owe someone rénqíng" is to be in their social debt. Gift-giving is one of the primary means of building and repaying 人情. The concept is inseparable from 关系.

Notes: 人 rén (person) + 物 wù (thing). A notable person, a "somebody," and also a character in a novel, film, or play: 历史人物 "a historical figure," 主要人物 "the main character."
人 rén + 缘 yuán (fate; karmic bond, a Buddhist term for the predestined connections between people). Literally: one's karmic bond with people. In practice: whether others naturally warm to you.

English: benevolence and love; humanitarian care; genuine concern for others
Notes: 仁 rén (humaneness) + 爱 ài (love; affection). The compound that captures 仁's essential motion: active, outward-reaching care for others. 仁 without 爱 is a concept; 仁爱 is what it looks like in practice.

Notes: 仁 rén + 慈 cí (tender care; the warmth of a mother for a child). The quality of someone whose inner humaneness produces visibly tender conduct. Warmer and more personal than 仁爱: 仁爱 can describe a principle, 仁慈 always describes a quality felt by the recipient.

English: humaneness and righteousness; moral conduct; the Confucian ethical pairing
Notes: 仁 rén (humaneness) + 义 yì (righteousness; moral rightness). The foundational pairing in Confucian ethics: 仁 is the inward quality of genuine care; 义 is the outward expression of doing what is morally right. Together they describe the full ethical person.

English: an army of benevolence and righteousness; a just and humane military force
Notes: 仁义 (benevolence and righteousness) + 之 (attributive particle) + 师 (army; force; teacher).

English: the humane person; one who possesses 仁 (classical)
Notes: 仁 rén + 者 zhě (the one who…; nominalizer in classical Chinese). The classical term for a person who has cultivated 仁.

English: to spot, to pick out, to identify (from a group or after a delay)
Notes: 认 rèn + 出 chū (out; resultative: to come into view). The act of identification , picking someone out of a crowd, recognizing a familiar face after years apart, identifying a body. The 出 marks the moment recognition crystallizes.

English: to admit one's mistake; (also) to mistake one thing for another
Notes: 认 rèn + 错 cuò (wrong; mistake). Two readings split by context. To acknowledge a mistake: 我向你认错 "I admit my mistake to you." To mistake X for Y: 我认错人了 "I had the wrong person" (lit. "recognized-wrong the person").

English: to recognize, to be able to identify
Notes: 认 rèn + 得 de (potential complement: be able to). Able to recognize. Slightly more colloquial than 认识 and emphasizes the act of recognition rather than ongoing acquaintance. The negative 不认得 "don't recognize" is very common.

English: to firmly believe; to be certain that; to officially determine
Notes: 认 rèn + 定 dìng (fixed; settled). Settled recognition. Two registers: personal conviction ("I'm certain that…") and official determination (a court, a regulatory body officially classifying something). Stronger and more committed than 认为.

English: to resign oneself to fate; to accept what is given
Notes: 认 rèn + 命 mìng (fate; lot; what Heaven decrees). To acknowledge one's fate. The act of accepting what cannot be changed: sometimes wisdom (Confucian 知命), sometimes resignation (giving up the fight). Tone depends on context.

English: to know (a person, a place, a character); knowledge, understanding
Notes: 认 rèn + 识 shí (to know; to discern). The standard verb for knowing-by-acquaintance: knowing someone, knowing a place, knowing a character. As a noun, it means understanding or grasp of a topic.

English: to concede defeat; to give in
Notes: 认 rèn + 输 shū (to lose). To acknowledge a loss , in a game, an argument, a contest of will. The negative 不认输 "refuses to give in" is one of the standard ways of praising tenacity.

English: to identify with; to agree with; identification
Notes: 认 rèn + 同 tóng (same; to be one with). To recognize as one's own: the verb behind identification in the social and psychological sense. 身份认同 shēnfèn rèntóng = identity (in the sense of self-identification with a group).

English: to think; to believe; to consider (one's view)
Notes: 认 rèn (to recognize; to take as) + 为 wéi (to be; to take as). Literally "to take X as [one's view of the matter]." The most common compound for expressing personal opinion in modern Chinese , 我认为 wǒ rènwéi (I think that...) is the standard opener for stating a perspective in speech or writing.

English: to acknowledge a debt; to own up to a commitment
Notes: 认 rèn + 账 zhàng (account; bill; debt). To acknowledge the account. Originally and literally a debt; figuratively, any commitment one is held to. The negative 不认账 "to refuse to own up" is the standard accusation against someone who reneges.

Notes: ISO 9001 is 质量管理体系认证 (the quality management system certificate). 验厂 (yànchǎng) is a factory audit, such as BSCI for social compliance. Check the certificate's 有效期 and that the company name matches the one you are contracting with.

English: to recognize characters; to be literate; to read
Notes: 认 rèn (to recognize; to identify; to acknowledge) + 字 zì. The act of visually identifying a character and knowing its reading and meaning. Implies the foundational literacy skill. 不认字 = illiterate (cannot read), a stark and socially significant label.
任何 means "any whatsoever" and, true to the system, needs 都 at the verb: 任何人都可以参加 (anyone may take part), 任何问题都欢迎 (any question is welcome).
任 rèn (to entrust; office, post) plus 命. To formally place someone in a role by official decree. The standard verb in government, corporate, and academic contexts for the act of appointment.
仍 réng (still, as before) + 然 rán (so). Marks that a state holds unchanged despite what might have altered it: 仍然 here, the situation is still thus. Close to 还是 háishì but more written.

Notes: 日 (rì, day) plus 报: a report issued every day. The suffix that names mastheads, as in 《人民日报》 (Rénmín Rìbào, the People's Daily) and 《广州日报》.

日 rì (day) + 常 cháng (constant; ordinary; everyday). The standard adjective for "everyday, routine, daily life." 日常生活 rìcháng shēnghuó = everyday life. 日常用语 rìcháng yòngyǔ = everyday expressions (a category every Chinese textbook includes). 日常工作 = daily work/routine.

Notes: 日光 (rìguāng, sunlight, daylight) + 灯 (lamp): a fluorescent tube, named for the cool daylight-white glow it gives. The long white strip light common in offices and kitchens.
日 rì (day) + 记 jì (record). A day-by-day record of one's own life and thoughts: 写日记 "to keep a diary." The 日 marks the daily rhythm of the writing.

Notes: 日 rì (sun; day) + 历 lì (from 曆, the calendar). The everyday word for a calendar as a physical or digital object: the thing on the wall or in your phone that lists the days. This is the 曆 branch of 历, fully about counting and displaying days. For the tear-off page-a-day kind, the same word applies.

English: capacity: how much a container or system can hold
Notes: 容 róng (to contain, to hold) + 量 liàng (amount). The maximum a vessel, device, or system can take in: a bottle's volume, a battery's charge, a hard drive's storage, a hall's seating. 电池容量 (battery capacity), 硬盘容量 (disk capacity), 存储容量 (storage capacity).

Notes: 容 róng (face; appearance) + 貌 mào (looks; outward form). A person's facial appearance, slightly literary in tone. Used to describe how someone looks, especially in careful or admiring description. Compare the plainer 长相 zhǎngxiàng used in casual speech.

English: to hold; to accommodate; to seat
Notes: 容 róng (to hold) + 纳 nà (to take in; to receive). To take something in and have room for it. Used for physical capacity (a stadium holding a crowd) and, by extension, for accommodating ideas or people into a group.

容 róng (to hold) + 器 qì (vessel; implement; utensil). A thing whose whole purpose is to hold. The general noun for any container, from a jar to a software data structure. 器 names a made object with a function; 容器 is the object made for holding.

English: to tolerate; to put up with; to endure
Notes: 容 róng (to hold) + 忍 rěn (to endure; to bear). To make room for something unwelcome and not act against it. Often carries a sense of restraint under strain: one tolerates because acting out would be worse. The object is typically a behavior, a fault, or a situation rather than a person directly.

English: to permit; to allow; to admit of
Notes: 容 róng (to allow) + 许 xǔ (to permit; to grant). To leave room for something to happen. Slightly more formal than the everyday 允许 yǔnxǔ, and it often appears in the negative (不容许, does not permit) or with abstract subjects such as time, rules, or circumstances that "do not allow" a thing.

容 róng (ample room) + 易 yì (easy; to change). The most common word built on 容, and a core HSK item. It carries two linked senses: a task is "easy," and an event is "likely" or "apt to happen." The shared idea is low resistance: with room to spare, the thing happens readily.

Notes: 溶 róng (to melt into liquid) + 解 jiě. To melt and break apart. The scientific verb for a substance dissolving in a solvent: 盐在水里溶解 = salt dissolves in water; 溶解度 = solubility. Here 解 keeps its most literal force, the breaking of a whole into dispersed parts, in the language of chemistry.

融 róng (to melt; to blend; to merge) + 化 huà (to dissolve). The standard verb for a solid melting into a liquid: snow, ice, butter, chocolate. Here 化 supplies its concrete physical sense, the turning of one physical state into another.

English: softness and yielding — the power of the apparently weak
Notes: 柔 róu (soft, supple) + 弱 ruò (weak). The Daodejing's counterintuitive teaching: the soft overcomes the hard, the yielding overcomes the rigid. Water is soft yet carves rock. The newborn is supremely soft and full of life; the corpse is rigid.
肉 (flesh) + 麻 (má, numb, tingling). The skin-crawling feeling of words too sweet or sentimental, the goosebumps of secondhand embarrassment.
肉 (meat) + 松 (sōng, loose, fluffy). Meat dried and shredded into airy fibers, scattered over porridge or buns.
肉 (flesh) + 体 (tǐ, body). The bodily, corporeal self, set against 精神 (jīngshén, spirit) or 灵魂 (línghún, soul).
肉 (flesh) + 眼 (yǎn, eye). The unaided eye of flesh, as opposed to a telescope or microscope.

English: like this; so; in this way
Notes: 如 rú (like) + 此 cǐ (this). A literary "like this, so," used both to point back at what was said and to intensify: 如此美丽 "so beautiful." The set phrase 原来如此 means "ah, so that's how it is."

English: as before; unchanged; as it always was
Notes: 如 (rú, to be like; as if , a woman and a mouth: to speak as the other speaks, to conform to) + 故 (gù, old; former). As before, unchanged since the past. 一切如故 (everything as before) describes a scene that time has not touched.
如 rú (suppose) + 果 guǒ (outcome). The default "if," opening the condition clause and usually answered by 就 jiù in the result: 如果你来，我就很高兴 "if you come, I'll be glad."

English: how; in what way; what about
Notes: 如 rú (according to) + 何 hé (what). The literary "how," asking by what means or in what manner: 如何解决 "how to solve it." The spoken everyday word is 怎么 zěnme; 如何 belongs to writing and formal speech.

Notes: 如 rú (like) + 同 tóng (same). A slightly literary way to say one thing is just like another, common in description and writing: 如同白昼 "as bright as day." In speech 好像 hǎoxiàng is the everyday equivalent.
如 rú (according to) + 意 yì (wish; intention). Turning out the way one hoped: 称心如意 "perfectly content." A staple of festive blessings, where 万事如意 wishes that every affair go as desired.

Notes: Founded by Confucius (孔子 Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BCE). Core values: 仁 rén (benevolence/humaneness), 礼 lǐ (ritual propriety), 义 yì (righteousness), 忠 zhōng (loyalty), 孝 xiào (filial piety).

English: to get started; to cross the threshold of a subject; a primer
Notes: 入 rù (to enter) + 门 mén (door). To step across the doorway of a field, to grasp its basics. A book titled 《汉语入门》 is "Chinese: A Primer," a doorway into the language.

English: when in a village, follow its customs — adapt to local ways
Notes: Lit: enter-village-follow-customs. The essential guide to cross-cultural conduct , observe and adopt local practices rather than imposing your own. Used practically and as a statement of cultural humility. 你到了那里，要入乡随俗 "When you get there, follow local customs."

Hotels must register foreign guests' passports, and not every hotel is licensed to take foreigners, so book one that confirms it does. 押金 (yājīn) is the deposit, 退房 (tuìfáng) checkout. For a company invoice, give the 抬头 (táitóu, the invoice name).

软 ruǎn (soft) + 件 jiàn (a piece). The intangible programs that run on a computer, paired against 硬件 yìngjiàn (hardware), 硬 yìng meaning hard. The soft and hard contrast is a direct calque of the English pair, with 件 supplying the shared unit-of-a-system sense.

English: shamanic dance — the body as ritual instrument
Notes: Shamanic dance (萨满舞 sàmǎn wǔ) is the physical form of the spirit-journey: the rhythmic movement of the body , spinning, jumping, mimicking animal spirits (bear-stomp, eagle-wing, snake-writhe) , accompanies and intensifies the drum-driven trance.
赛 (sài, to compete) + 跑. The verb-noun for a competitive run. 百米赛跑 (bǎi mǐ sàipǎo, hundred-meter dash) and 长跑赛 (chángpǎo sài, long-distance race) are the standard sports terms.

Notes: 三 sān + 餐 cān (meal). The three daily meals: breakfast (早餐 zǎocān), lunch (午餐 wǔcān), and dinner (晚餐 wǎncān). The phrase 一日三餐 (three meals a day) is the standard way to refer to daily sustenance, and by extension to reliable, ordinary livelihood.

English: the Three Bonds and Five Constants — the Confucian social order
Notes: The three bonds (三纲): ruler-minister, father-son, husband-wife. The five constants (五常): benevolence (仁), righteousness (义), ritual propriety (礼), wisdom (智), and trustworthiness (信). Systematized in the Han dynasty, this framework defined Confucian social structure for two thousand years.

English: the Three Kingdoms; the era of three rival states
Notes: 三 sān + 国 guó (kingdom; state; country). The Three Kingdoms period (220–280 CE), when China split into Wei (魏), Shu (蜀), and Wu (吴) after the collapse of the Han dynasty.

Notes: 三 sān (three) + 角 jiǎo (corner; angle) + 形 xíng. The three-corner shape. 形 is the standard suffix that turns a description into the name of a geometric shape: 正方形 zhèngfāngxíng (square), 圆形 yuánxíng (circle), 长方形 chángfāngxíng (rectangle).

English: three risings three fallings — Junshan Yinzhen's display
Three Pure Ones — the supreme triad of Daoist theology

English: to think carefully; to think three times before acting
Notes: 三 sān + 思 sī (to think; to reflect). From the Analects: 季文子三思而后行 , "Ji Wenzi thought three times before acting." Confucius's comment was that twice was already sufficient, but the wisdom of pausing before action became proverbial.

Sanxingdui , "Three Star Mounds," the Bronze Age archaeological site near Guanghan. The bronze masks, standing figure, and sacred tree uncovered there belong to a culture with no connection to the contemporaneous Shang dynasty. 堆 means "mound" or "pile."

English: three distances; three modes of spatial recession
Notes: 三 sān (three) + 远 yuǎn (far; distance). Guo Xi's taxonomy from 林泉高致 (1080s): 高远 gāo yuǎn (high distance -- looking up from base to peak, creates grandeur and vertical drama), 深远 shēn yuǎn (deep distance -- looking through receding layers of mountains and valleys, creates mystery and depth), 平远 píng…

Notes: 三 sān + 字 zì (character; written word) + 经 jīng (classic; canonical text). A classical primer written in three-character rhyming lines, composed in the Song dynasty and memorized by virtually every literate child in pre-modern China.

English: The "Sao style" , the poetic tradition derived from Qu Yuan's 离骚, characterized by longer lines, the medial particle 兮 xī, lavish botanical and spiritual imagery, and the theme of exile and unrecognized virtue. One of the two foundational styles of classical Chinese poetry.

English: tomb sweeping — the annual visit to the graves
Notes: 扫墓 (lit. "sweep the grave") is the Qingming practice of clearing the tomb of weeds and debris, adding fresh soil, pouring libations of wine, burning paper offerings, and sharing food at the grave site.

Notes: 山 shān (mountain) + 脚. The base of a mountain , where the slope meets the plain, where villages and trailheads sit. Standard geographical vocabulary.

山 shān + 脉 mài (vein; pulse; connected system, the word for pulse in traditional Chinese medicine). A mountain range as a vein of the earth, all peaks connected underground. Same logic as 水脉 (water vein) and 血脉 (bloodline). 秦岭山脉 the Qinling Mountains.

Notes: 山水 + 风光 (fēngguāng, scenery; views). The standard tourism and travel-writing phrase. 桂林山水甲天下 (Guìlín shānshuǐ jiǎ tiānxià, "the landscape of Guilin is first under heaven") is one of the most-quoted lines in Chinese tourism , a fixed praise-formula, originally a Song-dynasty poem.

English: landscape poetry; the mountain-and-water poem genre
Notes: 山水 + 诗 (shī, poem). The poetic genre that parallels the painting genre. Founded in the Six Dynasties period by Xie Lingyun (谢灵运, 385–433) and brought to its high point in the Tang by Wang Wei (王维) and Meng Haoran (孟浩然).

English: amid mountains and waters; in the landscape
Notes: A literary phrase widely used in modern essays, song lyrics, and travel writing. 之间 zhī jiān = between; amid. The phrase carries the Daoist resonance of being in the landscape rather than looking at it. Common in tea-house names, hotel names, and book titles aimed at evoking refinement.

善 shàn (good) + 恶 è (evil; bad). The paired terms that define the moral axis. In classical Chinese thought, 善 and 恶 are not absolute opposites in a cosmic war but positions on a continuum of conduct , and the line between them runs through every person, which is why cultivation matters.

Notes: 善 shàn (goodness) + 良 liáng (good; fine; sound). The most common compound in everyday speech for describing a person's character. 善良的人 = a kind-hearted person. 良 reinforces and grounds the abstraction of 善 into lived quality.

Notes: 善 shàn + 意 yì (intention; meaning). The moral quality of an act before it has been carried out: the intention behind the gesture. 出于善意 chūyú shànyì = "out of goodwill." Often appears in contexts where motives need to be clarified or defended.

English: to be good at; skilled in
Notes: 善 shàn + 于 yú (at; in; toward , a classical preposition that here marks the domain of competence). The most common modern compound for natural ability or cultivated skill. Takes a verb or activity directly: 善于 + 动词 verb phrase. Implies a degree of mastery, not just familiarity.

Notes: 伤 shāng (wound; injury) + 心 xīn (heart). Lit. "wounded heart." The heart as a physical organ that can be injured. Used for real losses: a pet dying, a relationship ending, a deeply disappointing outcome. Stronger and more pointed than 难过 nánguò (distressed, upset).

English: the marketplace is a rivers-and-lakes world — X是个江湖 as a productive formula
Notes: The formula X是个江湖 applies 江湖 logic , its hidden codes, dangers, unwritten rules, and webs of obligation , to any competitive domain.

English: to discuss: to talk something over, to consult
Notes: 商 shāng (to consult, to confer) + 量 liang (measure, toneless here). To talk a matter over with someone before deciding: to weigh it between two minds.

Notes: 商鞅 Shāng Yāng (c. 390–338 BCE), born in Wei, served as the chief minister of Qin under Duke Xiao from 356 BCE.

English: admiring chrysanthemums — the flower of late autumn resilience
Notes: 赏 shǎng (to appreciate; to admire) + 菊 jú (chrysanthemum). The chrysanthemum (菊花 júhuā) blooms in autumn, long after spring flowers have finished. This timing made it a symbol of resilience, longevity, and the virtuous person who thrives when others have withered.

English: social atmosphere; moral climate; the prevailing spirit of society

Notes: 社 shè (community) + 区 qū (district, zone). A bounded local community: the people of a single neighbourhood, plus the services and administration that serve them. 社区服务 "community services," 社区医院 "a community clinic," 社区活动 "neighbourhood activities." Smaller and more concrete than 社会.

社 shè (association) + 团 tuán (a group, a body). A voluntary organized group bound by a shared interest: 学生社团 "student clubs," 民间社团 "civic associations." The everyday word for the clubs and societies people choose to join, especially at school and university.

谁 (who) fronted before 都 universalizes over all persons. 谁都知道 = "everyone knows," with the implication that no person could be ignorant of this fact. Often carries a mild rhetorical force: the speaker is emphasizing how obvious or widespread something is.

什么 fronted before 都 universalizes over all things or all options. 什么都行 literally "anything goes" , no restriction exists. Extremely common in everyday speech for expressing total flexibility or total acceptance.

The question word "when," literally "what time/moment." It sits where the time answer would go, not at the front as in English: 你什么时候走？("When are you leaving?"). One of the core question patterns alongside 哪儿 (where), 谁 (who), 怎么 (how).
Ask about a word, not a person: "这个词是什么意思" is neutral, while a bare 你什么意思？ means "what are you implying?" and sounds hostile. Keep 这个词 in front.

English: a line of verse; lines of poetry
Notes: 诗 shī (poem) + 句 jù (line). A line or verse of poetry, the unit a poem is built and quoted in: 优美的诗句 "beautiful lines of verse." Often used in the plural sense, the lines of a poem taken together.
Sage Poet: honorific for Du Fu, whose verse embodied moral gravity and historical witness.

十 shí (ten) + 二 èr (two). The separator apostrophe in pinyin marks the syllable boundary: shí·èr, not shí·ér. Twelve is culturally loaded: 十二生肖 shí'èr shēngxiào (the twelve zodiac animals) and 十二个月 shí'èr gè yuè (twelve months) both run on this number.

English: the Twelve Muqam — Uyghur classical music tradition
Notes: The Twelve Muqam (木卡姆 mùkǎmǔ, from Arabic maqam, meaning mode/scale) is the comprehensive musical tradition of the Uyghur people: twelve suites, each a multi-movement composition comprising song, instrumental interlude, and dance, totaling hundreds of pieces.

十 shí (ten; complete) + 分 fēn (part; portion; to divide). Ten out of ten parts: the full measure of something. The most natural intensifier in formal and written Mandarin, sitting between 很 hěn (colloquial "very") and 非常 fēicháng (extremely, emphatic).
十 shí (ten) + 干 gān (stem; heavenly stem). The cycle of ten: 甲 jiǎ, 乙 yǐ, 丙 bǐng, 丁 dīng, 戊 wù, 己 jǐ, 庚 gēng, 辛 xīn, 壬 rén, 癸 guǐ.

十 shí + 年 nián (year). A decade. English: eight or nine times out of ten; most probably
Notes: 十 (ten) + 有 (have) + 八九 (eight or nine). Out of every ten, eight or nine, hence almost always, in all likelihood. A common way to state strong probability: 这件事十有八九是真的, "this is most probably true." The form 十之八九 (eight or nine out of ten) is equivalent.

十 shí + 月 yuè (moon; month). The standard Mandarin name for October and for the tenth month of any lunar calendar. Chinese month names are purely numerical: 一月 through 十二月, January through December. The naming system makes 十月 the last single-digit-ten month before 十一月 (November) and 十二月 (December).

十字 shízì (cross shape) + 路 lù (road) + 口 kǒu (opening; mouth). The point where two roads cross to form the shape of 十: a four-way intersection. Widely used both literally (traffic intersections) and metaphorically (a crossroads in life, a moment of decision between multiple paths).

Notes: 石 shí (stone) + 头 tou (suffix). The everyday word for a stone or rock. The bare 石 survives mostly in compounds and set terms; 石头 is the word you say out loud.

English: the spirit of the age; the zeitgeist
Notes: The defining outlook and values of an era, the calque that matches the German "Zeitgeist." 时代 (the age) plus 精神 (spirit). Used in cultural and political commentary to name what an age believes about itself: 把握时代精神 ("grasp the spirit of the times").

English: the right moment; timing; an opportune occasion
Notes: 时 shí (time) + 机 jī (machine; pivot; crucial moment; opportunity). 时机 is the Confucian classical meaning of 时 made into a compound: the moment that is ripe, when conditions align. It is strategic time, the narrowing window before it closes.

English: the plain future: tomorrow I go
Notes: A future time word with a bare verb is complete and idiomatic: 我明天去上海 (I'm going to Shanghai tomorrow), 下个月放假 (vacation starts next month). No marker is required at all.

实 shí (actual) + 践 jiàn (to tread; to carry out). The doing that turns an idea into action and tests it against reality: 理论与实践 "theory and practice," 实践证明 "practice has proven."

English: to put into practice; to implement (a policy, a system)

Experiment: to test against reality. 做实验 is to run an experiment; 实验室 is the laboratory; 实验中学 is the "experimental high school" found in nearly every Chinese city.

实 shí (real) + 在 zài (to be present). As an adverb it intensifies: 实在太累了 "I'm really exhausted." As an adjective it describes someone solid and unpretentious: 这个人很实在 "this person is genuine and reliable."
食 shí (to eat; food) + 物 wù (thing). Food as a category of substance, the general written term: 健康食物 "healthy food." For "a meal" you would say 饭 fàn, and for cooked dishes 菜 cài.

English: to use; to employ; to make use of
Notes: 使 shǐ (to cause; to employ; to dispatch) + 用 yòng (to use). The formal, neutral verb for using a tool, a resource, a method, or a right. Appropriate in written and professional contexts. English: generations; for generations; from age to age

世 shì (age) + 纪 jì (a record; a span of years). A hundred-year stretch of time: 二十一世纪 "the twenty-first century," 半个世纪 "half a century," 跨世纪 "spanning the turn of the century." The standard unit for dividing modern history.

世 shì (generation) + 袭 xí (to inherit; to succeed to). Passed down by birth from one generation to the next: 世袭制度 "the hereditary system," 世袭爵位 "a hereditary title." Marks a right or rank inherited through bloodline rather than earned or appointed.

是 (yes/right) + 否 fǒu (no; to negate , a classical negative particle). A formal, written-register conjunction meaning "whether or not." The colloquial equivalents are 有没有 or 是不是. 是否 appears in journalism, academic writing, formal correspondence, and polished speech.

English: Is that so? or "really?" Slightly cooler than 真的吗, often signaling polite interest without strong surprise. The neutral acknowledgment that you have heard and registered what was just said.

适 shì (to suit) + 当 dàng (to fit). Describes a measure, amount, or action that is right for the situation: 适当的时候 (at an appropriate time), 适当休息 (rest as appropriate).

English: to suit; to be suited to; to fit
Notes: 适 shì (to be apt) + 合 hé (to fit). A verb taking an object: X 适合 Y means X suits Y. 这本书适合孩子 "this book is suited to children."

English: to adapt; to get used to; to suit
Notes: 适 shì (to suit) + 应 yìng (to respond, to meet). To adjust oneself to new circumstances: 适应环境 (adapt to the environment), 适应新工作 (get used to a new job). The response here is the slow one of fitting in over time.

English: that which passes; the departed; what flows away
Notes: 逝 (to pass; to depart; to flow away) + 者. A thing-nominalization rather than a person-nominalization , 者 here points to an event or process rather than a human agent. This usage shows the full range of 者: it nominalizes any predicate, not just those describing human beings.

English: wristwatch: a watch worn on the wrist (錶 in traditional script)

手 shǒu (hand) + 机 jī (machine). China's most common word for mobile phone , the machine held in the hand. Completely replaced the earlier 手提电话 and the formal 移动电话 in everyday usage. 玩手机 wán shǒujī = "to play on one's phone" (ubiquitous activity).

Notes: 手 (hand) + 足 (foot). The literal limbs of the body, used figuratively for brothers or close companions. Classical Chinese: 手足之情 (shǒuzú zhī qíng, the feeling between hands and feet) means brotherly affection , your siblings are as necessary to you as your own hands and feet.

English: to defend the realm; to hold and preserve what was won
Notes: 守 shǒu (to guard; to protect; to hold steady , the character shows a hand over a roof, the posture of protection) + 江山. The harder and longer task: not the dramatic moment of conquest but the slow, unglamorous work of governing, maintaining order, and preventing the realm from unraveling.

English: conservative; set in old ways; resistant to change
Notes: 守 (shǒu, to guard, to hold onto , a hand over a roof) + 旧 (old). To guard the old order against change. In Chinese political and social discourse since the late Qing dynasty, 守旧 has been the standard term of criticism for those who resist modernization or reform.

English: the first time; for the first time
Notes: 首 shǒu (first) + 次 cì (time, occurrence). The first occasion on which something happens, common in news and formal writing. 首次访问 "a first visit," 首次公开 "made public for the first time." More formal than the spoken 第一次 dì-yī cì.

首 shǒu (head, chief) + 都 dū (metropolis, city). The head-city of a country, its seat of government. 中国的首都是北京 "China's capital is Beijing." Note the reading: here 都 takes its first tone dū (city), not the toneless dōu (all).

Notes: 首 shǒu (head, chief) + 领 lǐng (to lead; the neck, the collar). The leader of a tribe, band, or organization. Carries a slightly traditional or martial flavor: the chief of a clan, the head of an outfit. 部落首领 "a tribal chieftain."

English: first of all; firstly; in the first place
Notes: 首 shǒu (first) + 先 xiān (before, prior). The standard opener for an ordered list of points, often paired later with 其次 qícì (next) and 最后 zuìhòu (finally). Marks the very first item in a sequence of reasons, steps, or arguments.

English: prime minister (of a modern foreign government)
Notes: 首 shǒu (head; chief) + 相 xiàng (minister). The modern title for the head of government in countries such as Britain and Japan: 英国首相 "the British Prime Minister."

首 shǒu (first) + 要 yào (important). Marking the single most important matter, ranking above all others. 首要任务 "the primary task," 首要问题 "the chief problem." Stronger and more formal than 重要 zhòngyào (important), since it claims the top spot, not just high rank.

English: life-span; lifetime; (of a thing) durability, service life

特 tè (special; particular) + 长 cháng (strength; advantage, the area where one "goes long"). 你有什么特长？ "What are your special skills?" is the standard job interview form. 特长生 = a student admitted on the basis of a special talent (music, sports, art) rather than exam scores alone.

English: to raise; to improve; to enhance
Notes: 提 tí (to lift, to raise; to bring up) + 高 (high). To raise the level of something: 提高效率 (improve efficiency); 提高水平 (raise the standard); 提高工资 (increase wages). The standard verb for improvement in formal and professional contexts.

English: to move up in time; to do in advance; ahead of schedule
Notes: 提 tí (to lift; to bring forward; to raise up) + 前 qián (front; before). Literally "to lift forward": to move a scheduled event earlier than planned, to do something in advance. The opposite is 推迟 tuīchí (to postpone, to push back).

English: to ask a question; to raise a question
Notes: 提 tí (to raise; to bring up) + 问 wèn (to ask). To put a question forward, typically in a class or meeting. 老师提问 "the teacher asks a question," often of a student called on to answer.

English: exam question; title; subject (of an essay)
Notes: 题 tí (heading) + 目 mù (item; entry). The item set at the head of a test, or the title given to a composition: 考试题目 "exam questions," 作文题目 "the essay prompt." It points at the specific thing to be answered or written about.

English: to inscribe a poem (on a painting, wall, or scroll)
Notes: 题 tí (to inscribe) + 诗 shī (poem). To write a poem directly onto a surface, a classic gesture in Chinese painting where verse and image share one scroll.
题 tí (to inscribe) + 字 zì (characters). To brush words onto a painting, plaque, or wall, or the inscription itself. Often done by a respected figure as a mark of honor.

English: to grasp through experience; the understanding so gained
Notes: 体 tǐ (body) + 会 huì (to understand). To come to understand a thing by living it, and the insight that results. 深刻的体会 "a deep understanding (won from experience)."
体 tǐ (body) + 力 lì (strength). The body's stamina, the strength that sustains physical effort over time. Often paired against 脑力 nǎolì (mental effort): 体力劳动 "physical labor."

English: considerate; thoughtful; attentive to others' needs
Notes: 体 tǐ (to feel in the body) + 贴 tiē (to stick close). To feel another's situation closely and act with care: 体贴的丈夫 "a considerate husband." It is warmth shown through attention to small needs.

English: framework; structured system (of ideas or institutions)
Notes: 体 tǐ (body; structure) + 系 xì (connection). An organized framework, usually of something abstract: 理论体系 "a theoretical framework," 教育体系 "the education system." More architectural and conceptual than the everyday 系统.

English: to experience; to live through; an experience
Notes: 体 tǐ (body) + 验 yàn (to test, to verify). To know something by passing through it in person: 体验生活 "to experience real life." As a noun, the experience itself: 难忘的体验 "an unforgettable experience."

English: substance and function; essence and manifestation
Notes: 体 tǐ (body; substance; the underlying essence) + 用 yòng (function; use; the outward expression). A compound used in philosophy, aesthetics, Buddhist thought, and political theory to describe the relationship between a thing's nature and its operation in the world.
体 tǐ (body) + 育 yù (to nurture, to educate). The cultivation of the body: school PE, and sport in general. 体育馆 tǐyùguǎn is a gymnasium; 体育课 is a PE class.
体育 tǐyù (physical education, sport) + 馆. The roofed sports hall, as opposed to the open-air 体育场 (chǎng, a field/stadium). The 馆 marks the covered, indoor venue.

Constitution: one's inherent physical and energetic type, which determines predispositions to certain diseases and guides appropriate diet, lifestyle, and treatment choices. Nine constitutional types are defined in modern TCM standardization.

Notes: 体 tǐ (body) + 重 zhòng (weight). How much a person weighs: 量体重 "to weigh oneself." The weight that the body itself carries.

Notes: 替 (in place of) + 换 (swap). To take one thing out and put a stand-in where it was: a worn part, a player, a placeholder word. The replacement fills the same slot the original left.

天 tiān (heaven) + 才 cái (talent; ability). Heaven-bestowed ability , the kind of capacity that seems to have come from beyond ordinary human effort. The etymology encodes a theory of talent: genius is a gift, not a product.

English: the way of heaven; the natural moral order
Notes: 天 tiān (heaven; sky; the natural cosmic order) + 道 dào (way; path). The principle by which the cosmos operates: rewarding virtue, punishing tyranny, maintaining the balance of nature. An impersonal moral force, not a personal god.

English: between heaven and earth; in this world
Notes: 间 jiān (between; the space between two things). 天地间 names the space of human existence. A frequent location phrase in classical and literary prose.

English: Heaven, Earth, Humanity — the Three Powers (三才 sāncái)
Notes: The three constitutive powers of the cosmos in classical Chinese thought. Heaven (天) provides the patterns and conditions from above; Earth (地) provides the material ground and resources from below; Humanity (人) stands between them, participating in both and responsible for the mediation.

English: natural gift; innate ability; heaven's endowment
Notes: 天 tiān (heaven) + 赋 fù (to endow; to bestow; to compose, originally the government's levy on subjects, then poetic composition). Heaven's formal bestowal. 天赋 is slightly more formal and literary than 天才, referring to specific aptitudes rather than a person of exceptional overall genius.

English: heavenly stems and earthly branches; the traditional Chinese calendrical system
Notes: The 60-year calendrical cycle built on the same yang/yin cosmology that underlies 乾坤. 天干 tiāngān (heavenly stems): ten yang elements cycling through the years (甲 jiǎ, 乙 yǐ, 丙 bǐng, 丁 dīng, etc.).

Notes: 天 tiān (heaven) + 国 guó (kingdom; nation). The standard Chinese translation of "Kingdom of Heaven" in Christian scripture.

English: Tianhou Palace — her temples across the diaspora
Notes: After her elevation to 天后 (Heavenly Empress) by the Qing Emperor in 1683, Mazu's temples were formally renamed 天后宫 Tiānhòu Gōng (Tianhou Palace).

English: the celestial realm; heaven; the realm of gods and immortals
Notes: 天 (heaven; sky) + 界 (boundary; realm; world). The realm above 人间, populated by gods (神 shén), immortals (仙 xiān), and celestial officials. In folk-religion cosmology it mirrors the imperial bureaucracy below, with the Jade Emperor (玉皇大帝 Yù Huáng Dàdì) at its head.

English: the sky; the heavens as a physical expanse
Notes: 天 tiān (sky) + 空 kōng (empty; hollow; space). More poetic and specific than 天气: refers to the physical dome of sky above, not weather conditions. Used in literary contexts, poetry, and vivid description. 空 kōng also means "empty" , the sky is the great emptiness above.

Notes: 天 tiān (sky) + 气 qì (breath; air; vital force). Literally: the sky's breath. In traditional Chinese cosmology, qì 气 is the invisible force that animates all phenomena; weather is the sky breathing. HSK 1, but it carries this depth beneath the surface.

English: color of the sky; time of day as read from the light
Notes: 天 tiān (sky) + 色 sè (color; hue; appearance). The quality of sky-light as a way of telling the time or mood of the day: dawn's pale gray, midday's high white, dusk's orange bleed. A literary and slightly classical usage, common in classical fiction and poetry.

The Heavenly Mountains: the mountain range dividing northern and southern Xinjiang, with peaks reaching 7,443 m. A UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site, the Tianshan is the water source for the oasis cities of the Tarim Basin and one of the great mountain ranges of Central Asia.

Notes: 天 tiān (heaven) + 生 shēng (to be born; to live). "Born of heaven" = innate, not acquired. The counterpart to 后天 hòutiān (acquired; postnatal). In classical philosophy, the 先天/后天 dichotomy maps roughly onto nature/nurture, one of the most enduring debates in Chinese intellectual life.

Founded by Zhiyi 智顗 (538–597 CE) on Mount Tiantai 天台山 in Zhejiang. Tiantai's great achievement was doctrinal classification 判教 pānjìao: organizing all Buddhist scriptures into a hierarchical scheme of "five periods and eight teachings," with the Lotus Sutra 法华经 at the apex.

English: paradise; heaven as a place of bliss
Notes: 天 tiān (heaven) + 堂 táng (hall; grand hall; a place of gathering). The "heavenly hall," used in Chinese Buddhism for the Pure Land, and in general usage for any paradise-like place. Also commonly used hyperbolically: 美食天堂 (food paradise), 购物天堂 (shopping paradise), 自行车天堂 (cycling paradise).
Astronomy: heaven's patterns. 天文数字 ("an astronomical figure") is the standard idiom for an unthinkably large sum, same metaphor as English.

English: Heaven's movements are constant — the cosmos operates by regular, impersonal laws
Notes: 天 tiān (Heaven/Nature) + 行 xíng (movements, operations) + 有常 yǒu cháng (have regularity, are constant). The foundational statement of Xunzi's naturalism. Heaven's processes are reliable precisely because they are not subject to human will or divine whim.

English: to gaze into the distance; to look out over
Notes: 眺 tiào (to look afar) + 望 wàng (to gaze). To stand at a height and let the eye travel over a wide, distant view: 登高眺望 "to climb high and gaze out." More elevated and literary than ordinary 看, it implies an open vista and a lifted vantage point.

Notes: 铁 tiě (iron; steel) + 道 (way; path). The iron way: railway tracks as a path made of iron. Common in institutional and geographic contexts. Also 铁路 tiělù (the more common modern term for railway system). 铁道 tends to refer to the track itself; 铁路 to the railway as a transport network.

English: to comply with; to follow (advice, instructions)
Notes: 听 (to listen, to heed) + 从 cóng (to follow; to comply). To hear and act accordingly , to accept and follow guidance, instructions, or authority. Used for following medical advice (听从医嘱 tīngcóng yīzhǔ), following a superior's direction, or complying with a decision.

听 tīng (to listen) + 到 dào (arrive). Listening that arrived: the sound reached the ear and registered. 听到 is not an attempt to hear but a confirmed result. Compare 听 alone (the action of listening) with 听到 (the listening that succeeded).

English: to understand what one hears; to follow spoken language
Notes: 听 (to listen) + 懂 dǒng (to understand). The resultative complement 懂 marks successful comprehension , listening that reached understanding. Constant in language learning contexts: 你听懂了吗？ (Did you understand what you heard?) contrasts with 你听到了吗？ (Did you hear it? — did the sound reach you?).

English: obedient; to do as one is told
Notes: 听 (to listen) + 话 huà (words; speech). Obedient in the sense of listening to what is said and acting accordingly. The standard word for a well-behaved child: 这孩子很听话 (this child is very obedient).

English: to obey orders; to receive commands
Notes: 听 (to receive; to comply) + 命 mìng (command; order; fate). Used in military, official, and formal institutional contexts for strict compliance with authoritative commands. 听命于 (to obey the commands of; to be under the orders of).

English: to have heard (that); reportedly; I've heard that
Notes: 听 (to hear) + 说 shuō (to say; to speak). A hedging marker for secondhand information: "I've heard it said that…" Placed at the start of a clause to flag that the speaker did not witness the information directly. 听说他去北京了 (I heard he went to Beijing).

Notes: 听 (to listen) + 音乐 yīnyuè (music , 音 sound/tone + 乐 joy/music). The most common collocation for 听 in daily life. 听歌 tīng gē (to listen to songs) is the slightly more casual form.

The sustained-attention imperative with 着. 听 alone is a simple command to listen; 听着 adds the sense of "maintain that listening state." Common before announcements, reprimands, or instructions that require focused, continuous attention.

English: usually; ordinarily; generally; as a rule
Notes: 通 (general; holding throughout) + 常 cháng (constant; usual; frequent). The case that holds across most instances: usually, as the general rule. 通常 sets up the ordinary expectation against which exceptions are measured: 我通常七点起床 (I usually get up at seven).

English: to be open to traffic; to begin service (of a road or line)
Notes: 通 (to open; to be through) + 车 chē (vehicle). To be through to vehicles: the moment a new road, bridge, railway, or subway line opens and traffic can run along it. A staple of infrastructure news, where the opening of a line is itself an event: 正式通车 (officially opened to traffic).

English: to pass through; to get past; by means of; via
Notes: 通 (to go through) + 过 guò (to cross; to pass). The everyday verb for getting through something: passing through a gate, passing an exam, a motion passing a vote.

Notes: 通 (to connect; to convey) + 信 xìn (a letter; a message; trust). To get messages through to one another. Historically it meant to exchange letters: 我们通了多年信 (we corresponded for many years).

通 (general; running throughout) + 用 yòng (to use). Usable throughout, across cases: not specialized to one situation but serving generally. 通用 describes something accepted everywhere or applicable across the board: 全国通用 (valid nationwide), 通用规则 (a general rule that applies in all cases).

English: to notify; to inform; a notice; a notification
Notes: 通 (to get through; to convey) + 知 zhī (to know; to make known). To make something known by getting word through: the standard word for an official notification and the act of giving it. Works as a verb (请通知大家, please notify everyone) and a noun (一份通知, a notice).

English: at the same time; meanwhile; moreover
Notes: 同 tóng (same) + 时 shí (time). The same moment: 同时进行 "to proceed simultaneously." As a connector it also means "at the same time, moreover," adding a further point.

Notes: 同 tóng (same; together) + 行. The two readings split cleanly: tóngháng = "same trade" → a colleague, a competitor in the same line of work. tóngxíng = "to walk together" → to travel as companions. Same characters, two unrelated meanings , distinguished entirely by reading.
同 tóng (same) + 学 xué (study). One who studies alongside you. A teacher also uses 同学 to address a pupil: 这位同学 "this student here." 老同学 means an old schoolmate.

Notes: 同 tóng (same) + 样 yàng (kind). Of the same kind, used before a noun (同样的方法 "the same method") or as a sentence adverb meaning "in the same way, likewise."

English: to agree; to consent; to approve
Notes: 同 tóng (same) + 意 yì (idea; intention). To hold the same idea, to give one's assent: 我同意你的看法 "I agree with your view." The opposite is 反对 fǎnduì, to oppose.

Notes: 同 tóng (same) + 志 zhì (aspiration; will). One of the same aspiration. The standard revolutionary address for "comrade," and in contemporary informal use a self-chosen word for gay people.

Bronze man: the life-sized bronze figure commissioned in 1026 CE with channel lines and point locations engraved on the surface and a hollow interior. Filled with water and wax for examination purposes, it was the world's first standardized anatomical teaching model for acupuncture instruction.
童 tóng (child) + 话 huà (story). A tale told for children. Its kin 神话 shénhuà (god-story) means a myth, and 神话 and 童话 together cover the world of fabulous stories.

统 tǒng (to govern; to bind together) + 一. The political constant of Chinese civilization: 天下统一 (unification of all under heaven). As verb: 统一思想 (unify thinking), 统一标准 (standardize). As adjective: 统一规格 (uniform specifications).

Notes: 痛 (tòng), to ache, joins 苦 (kǔ), bitter, to name suffering felt in body or mind. The most direct word for anguish, it covers physical pain and emotional torment alike.

痛 tòng (pain; with full intensity) + 快 kuài (free-flowing; pleasurable). Two distinct but related uses. As a personality or speech descriptor: so direct and honest it cuts , blunt, refreshingly frank. As an experience descriptor: so wholly satisfying that nothing was held back.

头 tóu (head) + 发 fà (hair). The hair on a person's head, as a mass. Note that 发 here is the fà / 髮 reading; in casual speech the syllable often softens toward neutral tone. Distinct from 毛 máo, the word for body hair and fur.

English: the first seven-day memorial after death
Notes: 头 tóu (head; first) + 七 qī (seven). Traditional Chinese mourning involves rituals at seven-day intervals for 49 days , the period the soul is believed to linger. 头七 (day 7) is the most important: the family burns paper offerings and sets a place for the deceased at the table.

English: headache, can't go — circumstance prevents ability
Notes: 能 covers physical capacity (your body can or cannot do something) and circumstantial ability (the situation allows or does not allow).

English: to throw; to cast; to drop in
to vote: to cast a ballot
Notes: 投 tóu (to throw; to cast; to drop in) + 票 piào (slip; ballot). To vote, literally to throw a slip into the box. The image is exact: a ballot is a slip of paper, and casting it is dropping it into the urn.
突 tū (to dash out, abrupt) + 然 rán (-ly). Unlike 忽然, 突然 can also be a full adjective: 很突然 "very sudden," 突然的变化 "an abrupt change." So it covers both "suddenly" and "abrupt."

Notes: 图 tú (chart; image) + 画 huà (painting). A general word for a picture or illustration, the kind in a children's book or on a wall. Broader and plainer than 国画 or 油画, which name specific traditions.

图 tú (drawing; map; illustration) + 书 shū (book) + 馆 guǎn (hall; building for a function). A building for maps and books. The word 图书 túshū , "illustrated books" , is now the formal term for library holdings in general.

Notes: 图 tú (drawing; diagram) + 形 xíng. A drawn figure or graphic: shapes on a page, icons on a screen, the figures of geometry. 几何图形 = geometric figures; 图形界面 = a graphical interface. Where 形状 is a thing's shape, 图形 is a shape that has been drawn as such.

2D drawings with dimensions; 3D文件 or 3D图 (sān-D tú) for the model file, usually STEP. 以图纸为准 ("the drawing governs") is the sentence that settles arguments, so make sure the drawing is the latest version.

土 tǔ (earth) + 地 dì (ground). In everyday speech, land or soil: 土地肥沃 "fertile land." In folk religion it also names the 土地神 or 土地公, the humble local earth-god of a village or plot, the small-scale heir to the old 社 cult, honoured at modest roadside shrines.

English: the Earth God — most local, most beloved deity
Notes: 土地公 (also 土地神 Tǔdìshén, formally 福德正神 Fúdé Zhèngshén) is the deity of a specific patch of ground: a village, a neighborhood, a field, a shop. He is the lowest-ranking god in the celestial hierarchy and the most ubiquitous.

Notes: 团 (a tight cluster, a ball of people) + 队 (organized group). The modern office and startup word for a project team bound by a shared task.
团 tuán (round; group) + 结 jié (to bind). To draw a group tightly together into one body: 团结一致 "united as one." Used of teams, communities, and nations holding together against difficulty.

Notes: A friend made online, from 网 wǎng (net) + 友 yǒu (friend). A thoroughly modern coinage and an extremely common one. Note that 友 contracts here from 朋友, a regular pattern: 友 alone serves as the bound "friend" element in compounds (校友 alumnus, 战友 comrade-in-arms, 笔友 pen pal).
网 (wǎng, net) + 站 (station): a website, a fixed point on the internet. The everyday word for any site you visit, from a shop to a search engine.

English: going toward rebirth — the Pure Land term for death as aspiration
Notes: 往 wǎng (to go toward) + 生 shēng (life; rebirth). The Pure Land term for a practitioner's death, framed not as loss but as aspiration fulfilled.

望 wàng (to look far) + 远 yuǎn (far) + 镜 jìng (lens, mirror). Literally "a lens for looking far": the instrument that brings the distant near. 天文望远镜 is an astronomical telescope; 双筒望远镜 is a pair of binoculars. A neat transparent compound that reads itself.
危 (endanger) plus 害 (harm). The danger turned active: to damage or jeopardize something, and the resulting harm itself. Common with health, society, environment.
危 (danger) plus 机 (critical juncture). A crisis: the decisive, threatening turn in an economy, a relationship, an illness, a career.
危 (danger) plus 急 (urgent). Danger compressed by time: a situation that is both perilous and pressing, where a hospital patient or a battlefield hangs by a thread.

English: a dangerous building; a lofty tower
Notes: 危 (here in both senses) plus 楼 (multi-storey building). In modern use, a condemned structure unsafe to enter. In classical poetry the same word means a tall tower rising into the air, the older lofty reading of 危.
危 (danger) plus 险 (steep, perilous), a doubling of two height-and-hazard words into the standard everyday term for danger. Works as both adjective (this is dangerous) and noun (a danger).

威 wēi (authority, awe) + 望 wàng (esteem). The prestige that commands respect and deference, the standing of someone in a position of leadership: 树立威望 "to establish one's prestige." Stronger than plain reputation, it carries a sense of earned authority.

威 wēi (awe, authority) + 武 wǔ (martial). Powerful and commanding in bearing, mighty in a dignified way: 威武的将军 "an imposing general," 威武雄壮 "majestic and powerful." Describes the impressive, formidable presence of soldiers, guards, or anything built on a grand and strong scale.

微 wēi (minute; subtle; trace) + 小 xiǎo (small). Doubles the smallness: 微 already indicates near-invisibility (as in 微生物 microorganism, 微波 microwave), and 小 compounds that. Used for things at the scale of cells, particles, or imperceptible contributions. A higher register than 很小.
微 wēi (faint; slight; minute) + 笑 xiào (laugh/smile). A small, soundless laugh: the smile. The word that names the warm, closed-lipped expression, distinct from the open-mouthed 大笑.

English: a besieged city; to lay siege to a city
Notes: 围 wéi (to surround; to encircle) + 城 chéng (city). Literally an encircled city, both the act of besieging one and the besieged city itself.
围 (surround) + 困 (trap). The concrete, original sense: to ring something so it cannot break out. Used for armies besieging a city and, by extension, for floodwaters or crowds that cut people off.

English: to break the law; to act illegally
Notes: 违 wéi (to violate; to go against) + 法 fǎ (law). To step over the line the law draws: 违法行为 "an unlawful act." The mirror image of 合法, the foot landing outside the level mark.

A fixed sum payable on breach, such as late delivery. Under Chinese law a court or arbitrator can reduce it if it is far above the actual loss, so set it at a level you can justify. 赔偿 (péicháng) is compensation for actual loss.

唯 wéi (only; alone) + 一. Used before nouns: 唯一的选择 (the only choice), 唯一的儿子 (only son). Stronger than 只有 zhǐyǒu in its emphasis on singularity , the uniqueness is total, not merely circumstantial. In formal or literary contexts: 唯一真神 (the one true God, in religious translation).

伟 wěi (towering, magnificent) + 大 dà. The highest register of greatness, used for great historical figures, great achievements, and (frequently in political contexts) the greatness of the Party or state. In everyday speech it can be slightly ironic if overused.

伪 wěi (false, counterfeit) + 君子. A person who performs the outward markers of virtue without the inward character , the one who speaks of 义 while calculating 利. The word's force comes precisely from the prestige of what it negates.

卫生 wèishēng (hygiene) + 间 jiān (room). The polite, standard word for a bathroom in homes and public buildings. A common synonym is 洗手间 xǐshǒujiān.

卫 (guard) + 星: the guard star that attends a planet. Covers the moon, the GPS constellation, and the dish antenna (卫星天线). The Great Leap Forward idiom 放卫星 ("launching a satellite") still means announcing an inflated achievement.

English: for this reason; because of this; to this end
Notes: 为 wèi (for; on account of) + 此 cǐ (this; the aforementioned). A formal connective linking back to a preceding reason or context and introducing what was done in response.
