calligraphy arts writing classical history aesthetics culture

English: scenting — the process of infusing tea with flower fragrance
Tags: tea tisane herbal culinary tcm health

English: ought to; should; be obliged to
Notes: 应 yīng (should) + 当 dāng (be fitting). A modal of obligation, near-identical in meaning to 应该 yīnggāi but slightly more formal, so it shows up often in rules, contracts, and writing.
Tags: meaning timing society characters modal ability grammar permission communication

English: to cope with; to handle; to deal with
Notes: 应 yìng (to meet) + 付 fù (to hand over, to deal out). To handle a task or person, often a difficult one. Can carry a tinge of just getting through it: 应付考试 (manage to get through the exam), 应付了事 (do something perfunctorily just to be done with it).
英 yīng (outstanding; heroic; talent that flowers) + 明 míng (luminous). The compound used to praise rulers, commanders, and decision-makers of exceptional vision. 英明的领导 "an enlightened leader."

English: valiant and impressive; heroic in bearing
Notes: 英 yīng (heroic, outstanding) + 武 wǔ (martial). Of a person, valiant and impressive in look and manner, the brave, spirited bearing of a hero or a fine soldier: 英武不凡 "valiant and out of the ordinary." A literary, admiring word, often used of a young officer or commander.

Tags: literature novels classics classical song rebellion history dynasty han statecraft strategy

English: to welcome, to go out to meet
Notes: 迎 (yíng, to go toward) + 接 (to receive). You walk out to meet an arrival and bring them in. Often warm or ceremonial: greeting guests, soldiers, the new year.

Tags: color darkness symbolism cosmology nature weather

English: to own; to cherish; to hold close
Notes: 拥 yōng (to embrace; to hold close; to crowd together) + 有. More emotionally warm than 所有 or 具有. Suggests not just legal or abstract possession but holding something dear. Used for things of personal value: relationships, opportunities, qualities of character, cherished experiences.

English: third Ming emperor, builder of Beijing
Yongming Yanshou (904–975 CE) — Song dynasty Chan-Pure Land synthesis
Notes: The sixth patriarch of Pure Land and a major Chan master simultaneously, Yanshou embodied the Chinese Buddhist principle that the two traditions are not opposed but complementary.

Notes: 用 yòng (to use) + 法 fǎ (way). The way a thing is properly used, especially a word or a tool: 这个词的用法 "the usage of this word." Built on the same "way of doing" sense as 方法.

English: to study hard; to work diligently; to apply oneself
Notes: 用 yòng (to use; to deploy) + 功 gōng (effort; merit; achievement). To deploy effort , the literal meaning maps exactly onto the English "to apply oneself." Used particularly of students and academic work, but extends to any disciplined sustained effort.
Tags: mastery ability evaluation characters daoism philosophy daily-life grammar

English: to exert force; to use one's strength; hard (of physical effort)
Notes: 用 yòng (to use) + 力 lì (force). To put physical force into an action: 用力推 "push hard," 用力拉 "pull with all your strength." Describes how an action is done, with muscle behind it.

用 yòng (use; function) + 途 tú (route; destination; intended course). The destination of deployment: what something is for, where its use is headed. 用途 answers the question "what is this for?" and tends to describe a range of applications rather than a single act of using.

Tags: radical emotion mind virtue ethics knowing daily-life

Notes: 优 yōu (excellent) + 点 diǎn (point). A good point, a strength. Its exact opposite is 缺点 quēdiǎn, a shortcoming. Together they are the standard pair for weighing a person, plan, or product.

优质 yōuzhì (excellent quality , 优 excellent + 质 substance/quality) is the premium tier modifier. 打造优质产品 (to build premium products) is a common mission statement. Contrasts with 劣质产品 (lièzhì chǎnpǐn, inferior-quality products) , counterfeit or substandard goods.

尤 yóu (outstanding; especially) + 其 qí (that; those). "Especially that" , used to single out one item from a broader set as particularly true or notable. Appears before verbs, adjectives, or noun phrases. Roughly equivalent to "particularly" or "above all."

English: due to; owing to; because of
Notes: 由 yóu (from) + 于 yú (at; in). A formal, written near-synonym of 因为, marking the cause at the front of a sentence: 由于天气原因，航班取消了 "owing to the weather, the flight was cancelled." It pairs with 因此 rather than 所以.
Tags: logic cohesion meaning characters classical daily spoken language etiquette

Notes: 邮 yóu (post; mail) + 件 jiàn (a piece). Originally any item sent through the post. In everyday modern use it most often means email: 电子邮件 diànzǐ yóujiàn (electronic mail) is regularly shortened to 邮件. To send one is 发邮件 fā yóujiàn.
Tags: measure-words things meaning characters business communication technology vocabulary

English: postage stamp: a stamp for mailing letters
Notes: 邮 yóu (post; mail) + 票 piào (slip). A postage stamp: a tiny printed slip stuck to an envelope that stands for prepaid postage. It is 票 in miniature, a small piece of paper carrying a fixed value, and a favorite object of collectors (集邮 jíyóu, stamp collecting).
油 yóu (oil) + 画 huà (painting). The Western art of painting in oils, named for its medium. Its native counterpart is 国画 guóhuà, named for its nation rather than its material.
友 yǒu (friend) + 情 qíng (feeling). The bond of friendship. Close to 友谊 yǒuyì in meaning, but 友情 leans on the felt warmth, while 友谊 leans on the formal relationship.

English: to make sense; to be reasonable; that's a fair point
Notes: 有 yǒu (to have; there is) + 道理 dàolǐ (reason; logic). "To have reason," to possess the quality of making sense. One of the most common spoken responses to an argument you find convincing, used the way "fair point," "that makes sense," and "good point" function in English.

有 + 的 (nominalizing particle). Functions as an indefinite partitive , "some of [a set already mentioned or implied]." The pattern 有的…有的… (some…others…) distributes a set into contrasting subgroups and is one of the most natural ways to express "some people…some people…" in Chinese.

English: a bit; slightly (pre-verbal, negative or complaint coloring)
Notes: 有 + 点 diǎn (a dot; a small amount). Always appears before verbs and adjectives as a pre-modifier. The key nuance: 有点 carries a slightly negative or complaint-inflected tone. You use it for problems, inconveniences, or things that fall short.

Placed before an adjective (or a feeling-verb) to say something is "a bit / somewhat" that way, usually with a tinge of complaint or an unwanted state. 有点儿 + 累 / 冷 / 贵 / 难 = a bit tired / cold / expensive / hard. It describes a current condition the speaker finds slightly undesirable.
Tags: measure-words time food characters grammar degree comparison syntax

English: to be related; to matter; to have a bearing on
Notes: 有关系 means there is a connection, relevance, or effect between two things. 这跟我有关系吗？= "Does this concern me / affect me?" Used to establish relevance, causation, or connection. Contrast with 有关 yǒuguān (related to; concerning , slightly more formal, often in 有关部门, "relevant departments").
有 (to have) + 害 (harm): possessing the capacity to wound. Its antonym 无害 (wúhài) marks a thing as harmless. Frequent on labels and in science writing.

English: Keep in touch when you have time	Keep in touch when you have time." Slightly more open-ended than 改天再聊. Suggests that contact will resume when both schedules permit. Polite and standard.
Notes: daily spoken language etiquette

有 yǒu (to have) + 礼貌. The default form of approval for someone's social bearing. Applied across the age range , to children, colleagues, strangers, foreigners , and across formality levels. 这个孩子很有礼貌 ("this child is very polite") is a high compliment to the parents as much as to the child.

English: do you have? / is there? (A-not-A question)
Notes: The A-not-A question form of 有. Used both for possession ("do you have X?") and for existence ("is there X?"). In rapid speech, 有没有 is often compressed or the object follows immediately: 有没有时间？ Also used as a sentence-final tag: 你来过北京，有没有？ — "You've been to Beijing, haven't you?"

English: to have face; to be prestigious; to feel honored
Notes: To possess and display face , to be in a position of recognized prestige or to feel that your standing has been acknowledged or elevated. Certain possessions, positions, and associations give face: luxury goods, titles, famous friends, prestigious education.

有 yǒu (to have; to possess) + 名 míng (name; fame). To have a name that people know , the most common adjective for "famous" in spoken Mandarin. Neutral in register, works for people, places, dishes, and brands alike.

English: there is someone; someone (existential + indefinite reference)
Notes: 有 in the existential construction introduces a person into the discourse. 有人 can function as the subject of a following verb: 有人说… (Someone said…; There are people who say…). This is a common way to introduce an indefinite agent , "some people say," "someone thinks," "there are those who believe."

有 + 时 shí (time). One of the most basic time adverbs: "at some times; sometimes." Often appears in the paired pattern 有时…有时… (sometimes…sometimes…) to describe alternating or variable states. 有时候 yǒu shíhou is the slightly more colloquial form (literally "at some time-instances").
Sometimes, literally "there are times." Often shortened to 有时. The paired form 有时候…有时候… means "sometimes… and other times…," a neat way to describe alternating situations.

English: to be busy; to have something come up; to have a matter to attend to
Notes: 有 yǒu (have) + 事 shì. "Have a matter." Used to beg off (something has come up) or to flag that you need something from someone: 我有事找你 "I have something to discuss with you."

English: somewhat; to some extent; there is some degree of
Tags: grammar classical syntax passive literary particles confucianism analects

English: capable; purposeful; with ambition and scope to act; achieving
Notes: 有 yǒu (to have; to possess) + 为 wéi (action; doing; purposeful agency). The counterpart to 无为 , intentional, directed, deliberate action.

English: there's a problem; there's a question

Notes: 已 yǐ = already; the connection has used up its allotted length. A peaceful, fatalistic way to accept a relationship ending , romantic, platonic, or professional.

Notes: 缘分 yuánfèn (predestined affinity; see the dedicated entry) and 命运 mìngyùn (fate) are related but distinct. 缘分 is about connections between people, encounters that were meant to be. 命运 is about one's overall life trajectory, the arc of what happens.

English: reason; cause; the why behind something

English: dependent origination; origin; the arising through causes and conditions
Notes: The Buddhist technical term for pratītyasamutpāda , the arising of phenomena through causes and conditions. In everyday use, 缘起 also means simply "the origin" or "how something came about." Source, literally "source head." The Yangtze's source was definitively surveyed only in the 1970s–80s, deep in the Tanggula Mountains on the Tibetan Plateau. English: in the distance; a distant place
Notes: 远 yuǎn (far) + 处 chù (place; location). The place that is far away, viewed from where you stand. A positional noun used as a subject or object, always indicating a vague far-off point rather than a named destination.

English: remote antiquity; the distant ancient past

English: to keep far from; to stay away from; to leave behind

English: prime minister (of imperial times); chief minister
Notes: 宰 zǎi (to govern; to manage) + 相 xiàng (minister). The highest official under the emperor, charged with overseeing the government. A staple figure of historical drama and idiom.

Notes: 找 zhǎo (to search for; to look for) + 到 dào (arrive). Searching that arrived at its target: the thing was found. 找 alone is the act of searching; 找到 is the confirmed discovery. 找不到 (can't find it) and 找到了 (found it!) are extremely high-frequency in daily speech.

English: to look for a job; to job-hunt
Notes: The set phrase for job-hunting. 找 (to look for) plus 工作. Common in life and conversation, especially among graduates and people changing roles: 毕业以后我要找工作 ("after I graduate I'll look for a job"). The result of a successful search is 找到工作 ("found a job"), with 到 marking the achieved result.

English: Zhaozhou's dog — the gateway kōan of Chinese Chan
Notes: Master Zhaozhou Congshen 赵州从谂 (778–897 CE) was asked: "Does a dog have Buddha nature?" He replied: 无 wú. Since Buddhist doctrine holds that all sentient beings have Buddha nature, "no" is doctrinally wrong , but so is "yes" if it's merely conceptual.
照 zhào (to shine upon; to illuminate) + 明 míng (bright). Used for artificial lighting systems, stage lighting, and the act of shining a light on something. 照明设备 = lighting equipment.
照 zhào (to shine; to reflect) + 相 xiàng (appearance). To fix a likeness in a picture: 给我照相 "take a photo of me." A separable verb: 照了一张相 "took one photo."

至 zhì (to reach; at the extreme of) + 少 (few, little). At the minimum: "reaching the least amount." 至少要三天 (it'll take at least three days); 至少有一百人 (at least a hundred people). The counterpart is 至多 zhìduō (at most). 至少 sets a floor; 至多 sets a ceiling.

Notes: 主 zhǔ (master; to take charge) + 动 dòng (to act). To move first and on one's own, rather than waiting to be pushed. Its opposite is 被动 bèidòng (passive). 主动帮忙 "to help without being asked."

注 zhù (to annotate; to gloss) + 脚. Annotation at the foot of the page. A more elegant alternative to the modern compound 脚注 jiǎozhù (which has the same components in reverse order).

English: to fix one's gaze; to give attention to
Notes: 注 (to pour into; to concentrate) + 目 (eye). To concentrate the eye on something. A formal register word for focused attention: 引人注目 yǐn rén zhùmù means "eye-catching" or "attention-drawing."

English: to pay attention; to take note; to watch out

English: to bless; to wish someone well; best wishes
Notes: 祝 zhù (to wish; to pray for) + 福 fú (blessing). To send blessings to someone, as a verb or noun. 送上我的祝福 = "I send you my best wishes." Standard in holiday messages, weddings, and farewells.

English: grasp firmly; make the most of (time)
Notes: 抓 (zhuā, to grab) + 紧 (tight). To grab and hold with no slack. Literally to grip something hard, figuratively to seize time and not waste it: 抓紧时间 (zhuājǐn shíjiān), make the most of the time.

专 zhuān (to specialize; sole) + 业 yè (field of study). As a noun, the major one studies: 我的专业是历史 "my major is history." As an adjective, professional or specialized: 专业知识 "specialized knowledge," 很专业 "very professional."

to transform; to convert; to change from one form into another
Notes: 转 zhuǎn (to turn; to shift) + 化 huà (to transform). 转化 names a conversion across a boundary: one form, type, or state turning into another. It is the standard word in science, philosophy, and economics for systematic conversion, the conditions under which A becomes B.

Notes: The canonical existential 有 structure. Place word or place phrase comes first, followed by 有, followed by the indefinite thing being asserted to exist. The place functions as the topic , the frame within which existence is being asserted.

字 zì (individual character) + 典 diǎn (canon; standard reference; classic text). A dictionary organized by radical, stroke count, or pronunciation that defines individual characters. The 典 suffix appears in 经典 jīngdiǎn (canonical classics); a 字典 is a canonical reference for individual characters.

字 zì (character) + 母 mǔ (mother; source; matrix). Literally: "character-mothers," the foundational elements of an alphabetic system from which all words are born. The term applies to any alphabetic system: the English alphabet, the pinyin romanization system, the Cyrillic alphabet.

字 zì (character; text) + 幕 mù (curtain; screen, as in 银幕 yínmù, the silver screen). Literally: "character-curtain." The text that appears across the screen like writing on a curtain. A modern compound that elegantly extends the ancient components into a contemporary context.

字 zì (character) + 体 tǐ (body; form; style). The physical form a character takes, whether in print, on screen, or in handwriting. Covers both digital fonts and handwriting styles. The same character can appear in multiple 字体: the same 字, different bodies.

English: the key word; the word one fastens on
Notes: 字 zì (character; word) + 眼. The eye of the phrase , the single word that carries the weight, that you pivot a sentence on, that an opponent picks at. 抠字眼 kōu zìyǎn "to pick at the wording" (often pejoratively, like English "splitting hairs over phrasing").
自 zì (self) + 传 zhuàn (a life record). A biography written by its own subject, the story of a life told in the first person: 写自传 "to write an autobiography." Like 传记, it takes the zhuàn reading.

English: ever since; from the time that
Notes: 自 zì (from) + 从 cóng (from; since). A conjunction marking a starting point in the past, paired with a later clause: 自从他来了以后 "ever since he arrived." Used only of time already begun, never the future.

English: self-aggrandizing; thinking oneself greater than one is; conceited
Notes: 自 zì (self) + 大 dà (great; large; important). Consistently negative , the failure of accurate self-assessment in the direction of inflation. Where 骄傲 can sometimes be legitimate pride, 自大 always describes a distortion: the person who claims more importance than they possess.

English: automatic; automatically; of one's own accord
Notes: 自 zì (self) + 动 dòng (to move). Moving by itself, without anyone working it: 自动门 "automatic door," 自动售货机 "vending machine." Also of people acting unprompted: 自动报名 "to sign up on one's own."

English: oneself; myself, yourself, himself (etc.); one's own
Notes: 自 zì (self) + 己 jǐ (oneself). The everyday reflexive word, flexing to whatever person the sentence needs: 我自己 "myself," 你自己 "yourself." It also marks possession, 自己的房间 "one's own room," and stresses doing a thing without help.

English: one of us; an insider; our own people
Notes: 自己 zìjǐ (oneself) + 人 rén. Someone who belongs to your group: your team, your family, your circle of trust. The implied contrast is always 外人 wàirén (outsider). 都是自己人，不用客气 "We're all family here, no need for formality" is an expression of warmth that lowers the social register instantly.

自 zì (self; one's own) + 家 jiā (family; home). Marks something as belonging to or originating from one's own household. Central to the Chinese social concept of insiders vs. outsiders: 自家人 (one of our own) vs. 外人 wàirén (an outsider).

English: complacent; self-satisfied; smug; resting on one's laurels
Notes: 自 zì (self) + 满 mǎn (full; satisfied). The state of being full , too full to receive more, too satisfied to keep improving. The classical warning 满招损 is precisely directed at 自满.

English: naturally and inevitably; of its own accord
the natural world; the realm of nature
to turn oneself in; to confess to the authorities
Notes: 自 zì (oneself) + 首 shǒu (to bow the head, to confess). To give oneself up to the law of one's own accord, before being caught. A legal term: voluntary surrender that often earns a lighter sentence. The head bows itself before justice.

English: the self; the ego; self- (in compounds)
Notes: 自 zì (self) + 我 wǒ (I; me). The self as an inner concept, the "ego" of psychology and philosophy. As a prefix it forms self-directed actions: 自我介绍 "self-introduction," 自我批评 "self-criticism."

Notes: 自 zì (self) + 信 xìn (to trust; believe). To trust in oneself: 他很自信 "he is very self-assured." A close cousin is 自尊 zìzūn (self-respect), another of the many self- compounds built on 自.
The most prototypical 被 sentence. Theft is unwanted, the subject (bicycle) is the victim, the agent (the thief) may or may not be named. The 了 marks the completion of the unfortunate act.
自 zì (self) + 由 yóu (to follow; from). Literally "following from oneself," to act from one's own will rather than another's: 言论自由 "freedom of speech," 行动自由 "freedom of movement."
宗 zōng (ancestor; lineage) + 教 jiào (teaching). The general word for religion, the handed-down teaching that a community is built around: 宗教信仰 "religious belief."

宗族 is the term for the patrilineal descent group: all those who share a common named male ancestor and who collectively maintain the ancestral hall and genealogy. In rural China, entire villages are often single-lineage settlements (单姓村 dān xìng cūn), with all residents sharing a surname.
综 zōng (to gather; to sum) + 合 hé (to join). To draw many parts into one comprehensive whole: 综合考虑 "to consider comprehensively," 综合大学 "a comprehensive university."
In short or "all in all." Conclusion marker that wraps up an explanation. Signals you have said your piece and are now landing the summary: 总之, 我觉得不错 ("all in all, I think it's fine").

Sticky rice dumplings wrapped in bamboo or reed leaves, traditionally triangular or cylindrical. Made with various fillings: red bean paste, salted egg yolk, cured pork. The characteristic food of the Dragon Boat Festival, eaten to commemorate Qu Yuan.

English: to travel the whole world; to have been everywhere
Notes: 走遍 zǒu biàn (to walk/travel all over; to cover thoroughly , 遍 is a comprehensive coverage complement) + 天下 (all under heaven; the whole world). The ambition of the traveler: to have seen everything, to have left no corner of the world unvisited.

English: to walk out of; to emerge from
Notes: 走 zǒu (walk; leave) + 出 (exit complement). The most neutral directional compound: walking across a threshold from inside to outside. Used for physical exits and metaphorical ones , 走出困境 (walk out of a difficult situation), 走出阴影 (emerge from the shadow of something).

走 zǒu (walk; go) + 道 (way; path). The path you walk: a corridor between rooms, an aisle on a plane or train, a narrow walkway between structures. Practical and architectural: the space designated for movement through an enclosed or constrained area.

English: to use personal connections to get something done
Notes: 走 zǒu = to go through; to travel via. 走关系 means to go through the channel of personal connections to accomplish something that might otherwise be difficult or slow.

Literally "going through the back door": using gifts and personal relationships to obtain favors, preferential treatment, or access that would not be available through formal channels. The phrase acknowledges the reality of this practice without fully endorsing it.

English: to travel the roads making a living; to hustle; to work itinerantly
Notes: Traditional use: traveling performers, fortune-tellers, medicine sellers, acrobats , people who made their living moving from town to town, outside the settled economy.

走 zǒu (to walk/go) + 路 lù (road; path). To walk , the action of foot-travel. 走路去 = to walk there (contrast: 开车去 to drive, 坐地铁去 to take the subway). Also used metaphorically: 走上了一条不归路 "walked a road of no return" · 走对了路 "took the right path (in life)." 请走路 = "please use the footpath" (on signs).

English: to move toward; trend; the run or layout of something
Notes: 走 zǒu (to go) + 向 xiàng (toward). As a verb, to head toward an outcome: 走向成功 "to head toward success." As a noun, the trend or physical run of a thing, as in the 走向 of a mountain range or a market.

English: to lease, to rent on loan
Notes: 租 (to rent) + 借 (to borrow). A bound compound for taking something for temporary use, often with a fee: leasing land, chartering equipment, the historical "leased territories" (租借地) of treaty-port China.

足 (foot) + 迹 (trace, mark). The imprint a foot leaves , both physical footprints and the metaphorical traces left by a life or a civilization. 留下足迹 (to leave one's footprints); 遍布全国的足迹 (footprints spread across the whole country).
足 (foot) + 球 (ball). The foot-ball: soccer in China and Taiwan. The Chinese Football Association (中国足球协会) governs 足球 nationally.

English: clan genealogy — the lineage's living memory
Notes: 族谱 (also 家谱 jiāpǔ or 宗谱 zōngpǔ) is the written genealogical record of a lineage. It records birth, death, marriage, official appointments, and notable achievements of every member, generation by generation.
祖 zǔ (ancestor, forebear) + 父 fù (father). The father's father, in formal register. Spoken Mandarin uses 爷爷 yéye for the same man, the way 爸爸 stands in for 父亲.

English: the day series, and its symmetric siblings

English: the left side; on the left
Notes: 左 (left) + 边 (side; edge). The most neutral, everyday word for "the left side." Used in directions, descriptions of position, and navigation. 在左边 (on the left), 左边的门 (the door on the left). Paired with 右边 yòubiān (the right side) for balanced descriptions of both sides of something.

English: sitting meditation — the formal practice of Chan
Notes: 坐 zuò (sit) + 禅 chán (dhyāna). Extended periods of seated meditation , in Japan called zazen 坐禅. Chan monasteries typically structure the day around multiple periods of 坐禅, sometimes lasting hours in intensive retreats (禅七 chán qī, seven-day intensive).
做 zuò (to make) + 菜 cài (dish). To cook, in the sense of making the dishes for a meal. 他很会做菜 "he is a good cook." Its near-neighbor 做饭 zuò fàn frames the same act around the staple rice.
